## Overview

Backpressure in a streaming pipeline is the mechanism by which a slow downstream consumer signals an upstream producer to reduce its emission rate, rather than letting an unbounded buffer grow until the process runs out of memory.

This mechanism is crucial in streaming systems to maintain stability and prevent resource exhaustion when data arrives faster than it can be processed downstream.

## Common Implementations

### Bounded Queues

The producer writes to a queue with a fixed size limit. Once the queue is full, the producer blocks until the consumer processes items and frees up space. This simple approach naturally prevents unbounded growth at the cost of blocking the producer.

### Credit-Based Flow Control

In credit-based models, the consumer explicitly grants the producer permission to send N more items. The producer tracks available "credits" and must wait for the consumer to return more credits before continuing to emit. This approach decouples producer and consumer timing while maintaining strict control over queue depth.

### Reactive-Pull Models

Rather than the producer pushing items to the consumer, the consumer requests items on its own schedule. The producer only emits when explicitly requested, making it impossible for the consumer to be overwhelmed. This is the model used by reactive systems and pull-based architectures.

## Benefits

- Prevents memory exhaustion from unbounded buffers
- Maintains system stability under bursty or uneven load
- Allows graceful degradation rather than cascading failure
- Enables fair resource allocation between producers and consumers
